lead: Correlative coding (partial-response signalling) adds a small, known ISI on purpose, so binary data can be sent at the Nyquist rate through a filter that can actually be built; duobinary, ck = ak + ak−1, is the standard example. M-ary PAM instead sends log₂M bits on each symbol by using M amplitude levels, cutting the bandwidth for a given bit rate at the cost of more power. PAM4 now carries 400G Ethernet.
prereq: You need: raised cosine bandwidth and error probability with Q(x).

blocks.text: Zero ISI in R<sub>s</sub>/2 needs the brick-wall sinc. Duobinary lets each sample hold the current symbol plus one copy of the previous one. With polar symbols a<sub>k</sub> = ±1 the coder output is
Here in delay-operator notation the coder is 1 + D, where D is a delay of one symbol.

With an ideal Nyquist filter the overall response is H(f) = 2T cos(πfT) e<sup>−jπfT</sup> for |f| ≤ 1/(2T). It falls smoothly to zero at the band edge, so a real filter can approach it, and the band is still R<sub>s</sub>/2. In time it is two sinc pulses T apart, whose sum decays as 1/t².

Undoing the coder by subtraction, âk = ck − âk−1, lets one wrong decision corrupt every later one: error propagation. The precoder prevents it. Before the coder, form the binary sequence pk = bk ⊕ pk−1 (⊕ is XOR), starting from p0 = 0, and send ak = 2pk − 1.

items: Precode: p<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub>, with p<sub>0</sub> = 0.
Map to polar: a<sub>k</sub> = +1 if p<sub>k</sub> = 1, −1 if p<sub>k</sub> = 0.
Receiver: if |c<sub>k</sub>| < 1 decide b̂<sub>k</sub> = 1; if |c<sub>k</sub>| > 1 decide b̂<sub>k</sub> = 0.

blocks.text: It works because c<sub>k</sub> = 0 exactly when a<sub>k</sub> ≠ a<sub>k−1</sub>, that is when p<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> = 1. Each decision uses only the current sample, so one level error gives one bit error.

sections.h3: Modified duobinary and the noise cost

blocks.text: Duobinary's spectrum is largest at f = 0, which transformer-coupled lines cannot pass. Modified duobinary uses ck = ak − ak−2, the operator 1 − D²: its response 2T sin(2πfT) is zero at both f = 0 and f = 1/(2T). Its precoder is pk = bk ⊕ pk−2, and the receiver decides b̂k = 1 when |ck| > 1.

The price is noise margin. The middle level has two thresholds to cross instead of one, and the 1 + D shaping, split equally between the transmit and receive filters, costs extra transmitted energy for the same level spacing. With that split and symbol-by-symbol decisions, the error probability is
Here the 1.5 counts the two thresholds of the middle level, and (π/4)² is an SNR loss of 20 log₁₀(4/π) = 2.1 dB against polar binary.
At E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 10 dB this gives 1.5 Q(3.512) = 3.33 × 10⁻⁴, against 3.87 × 10⁻⁶ for ideal binary. A sequence detector (Viterbi) instead of the slicer wins most of it back.

M-ary PAM sends one of M amplitudes per symbol, ±d, ±3d, …, ±(M − 1)d, so neighbours are 2d apart. Rs = Rb/log₂M and B = (Rs/2)(1 + α). The receiver needs M − 1 thresholds midway between levels. With Gray labelling neighbours differ in one bit, so BER ≈ Pe/log₂M.
Here E<sub>s</sub> is the average symbol energy (d² for binary, 5d² for 4-PAM), with E<sub>s</sub> = E<sub>b</sub> log₂M.
Inner levels have two boundaries d away, end levels one. With noise variance N₀/2,
Here for M = 2 this is Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)), the polar result.

For the same error rate E<sub>b</sub> must grow by (M² − 1)/(3 log₂M): 2.5 times (4.0 dB) for 4-PAM, 7 times (8.5 dB) for 8-PAM, 21.25 times (13.3 dB) for 16-PAM. The table gives E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ for P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵.

examples.question: The bits b<sub>1</sub> … b<sub>8</sub> = 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 are sent by precoded duobinary with p<sub>0</sub> = 0 (so a<sub>0</sub> = −1). Find p<sub>k</sub>, a<sub>k</sub>, c<sub>k</sub> and the decoded bits. Then show what a receiver without the precoder does when one level is misread.
steps: Coder: c<sub>1</sub> = +1 + (−1) = 0, c<sub>2</sub> = +2, c<sub>3</sub> = 0, c<sub>4</sub> = 0, c<sub>5</sub> = +2, c<sub>6</sub> = +2, c<sub>7</sub> = 0, c<sub>8</sub> = −2.
Decode: |c| < 1 gives 1, |c| > 1 gives 0: 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0, the bits sent.

If c<sub>4</sub> is misread as +2 the precoded receiver loses only b̂<sub>4</sub>. Without the precoder (c<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> + b<sub>k−1</sub>: 1 1 1 2 1 0 1 1), misreading the fourth level as 1 and decoding by b̂<sub>k</sub> = c<sub>k</sub> − b̂<sub>k−1</sub> gives 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, −1, 2, −1: every value from the error on is wrong.
examples.answer: p = 1 1 0 1 1 1 0 0, c = 0 2 0 0 2 2 0 −2, decoded 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0; a level error then costs one bit, while without the precoder it spreads to every later bit.

examples.question: A link must carry 9600 bit/s with a raised cosine of α = 0.25. Compare binary PAM and Gray-coded 4-PAM: symbol rate, bandwidth, thresholds, P<sub>e</sub> at E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 10 dB, and the E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ for P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵.
steps: Binary: R<sub>s</sub> = 9600 baud, B = 4800 × 1.25 = 6000 Hz, one threshold. 4-PAM: R<sub>s</sub> = 4800 baud, B = 2400 × 1.25 = 3000 Hz, three thresholds (0 and ±2d).
For 10⁻⁵: binary 9.59 dB; 4-PAM solves 1.5 Q(x) = 10⁻⁵, x = 4.355, E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = x² × 15/12 = 23.7, that is 13.75 dB.
examples.answer: Binary: 9600 baud, 6000 Hz, 1 threshold, P<sub>e</sub> = 3.87 × 10⁻⁶ at 10 dB, needs 9.59 dB. 4-PAM: 4800 baud, 3000 Hz, 3 thresholds, P<sub>e</sub> = 3.51 × 10⁻³ at 10 dB, needs 13.75 dB. Half the bandwidth costs about 4.2 dB.

traps: Decoding duobinary without a precoder by subtraction: one wrong level then corrupts every later bit.
Decoding precoded polar duobinary the wrong way round: c<sub>k</sub> = 0 means b<sub>k</sub> = 1, and ±2 means b<sub>k</sub> = 0.
Thinking duobinary's three levels carry more bits. One input bit still makes one symbol; the gain is a buildable filter at R<sub>s</sub>/2, and the cost is 2.1 dB.
Using M thresholds for M-PAM. There are M − 1.
Quoting the per-symbol energy ratio (5 for 4-PAM, 7 dB) as the power penalty. Compare per bit at the same error rate: 4-PAM needs about 4 dB more E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ than binary.

quiz.q: What are the output levels of a duobinary coder with polar input ±1, and what is its delay-operator form?
quiz.a: c<sub>k</sub> = a<sub>k</sub> + a<sub>k−1</sub> takes −2, 0, +2; the coder is 1 + D.

quiz.q: Why is a precoder placed before the duobinary coder?
quiz.a: Without it the receiver must subtract its previous decision, so one error propagates. With p<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub> each bit is read from the current level alone (|c<sub>k</sub>| < 1 means 1), so one level error gives one bit error.

quiz.q: A source sends 64 kbit/s through 8-PAM with α = 0.5. Find the symbol rate and the bandwidth.
A 16-PAM system has levels ±d, ±3d, …, ±15d with d = 0.5 V. Find the mean squared level and compare it with binary at the same d.
quiz.a: Mean squared level = (M² − 1)d²/3 = 255 × 0.25/3 = 21.25 V². Binary at the same d gives d² = 0.25 V², so 16-PAM needs 85 times the symbol energy (19.3 dB) for the same spacing.

quiz.q: Duobinary and ideal binary both reach 2 bit/s/Hz. Explain what duobinary gains and what it pays.
quiz.a: Both send one bit per symbol in R<sub>s</sub>/2. Binary needs the unbuildable brick-wall sinc; duobinary's cos-shaped response falls to zero at the band edge and can be built. It pays with three closer levels, a 2.1 dB SNR loss with symbol-by-symbol decisions.

beyond: Partial-response maximum-likelihood (PRML) detection, a partial-response channel followed by a Viterbi detector, read data from hard disks for decades. PAM4 carries 50 and 100 Gbit/s per lane in data-centre Ethernet. Search for PRML, Tomlinson-Harashima precoding and PAM4 eye diagram.
